entries.title: AI-generated lawsuits flood German courts
entries.summary: German courts are being overwhelmed by AI-generated lawsuits, many riddled with errors and running to huge lengths. Some state justice ministers want to introduce a fee to stem the flow, but that brings its own problems.
entries.content:
November 28, 2026

German courts are being overwhelmed by AI-generated lawsuits, many riddled with errors and running to huge lengths. Some state justice ministers want to introduce a fee to stem the flow, but that brings its own problems.

German courts are reporting a huge rise in lawsuits and complaints, and are blaming the use of artificial intelligence models.

The German media has been filled with reports about the problem, which particularly affects social courts, where citizens can file complaints themselves without legal representation. In most such cases, people appeal against sanctions or cuts to their unemployment benefits, or demands from authorities that benefits be returned, but the complaints can also pertain to other benefits or sudden rises in health insurance contributions.

Marcus Howe, spokesperson for Berlin's state social court, where he is himself a judge, said his court was dealing with 28% more cases this year than in 2025.

"That is of course an enormous increase, which is surely in part because of artificial intelligence," he told DW, though he added that it could also be partly down to the tightening of sanctions on unemployment benefits, introduced by the federal government this year.

Other states have reported similar increases. The Legal Tribune Online news portal reported that the number of urgent proceedings at the eight social courts in North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany's most populous state, rose from around 1,400 in the first quarter of 2025 to 3,600 in the same period of 2026.

How to spot an AI lawsuit

Howe said that in most cases it's still easy for judges to see when a complaint has been generated by AI.

"You can usually tell at first glance," he said. "The font and the layout are different. In the worst cases, they're much too long and bloated, stuffed with content that has very little to do with the case."

Howe has also noticed that the AI-generated lawsuits are more impersonal, which makes his job more difficult.

"You don't really get an impression of what kind of people are behind these cases," he said. "And it becomes difficult to recognize what the actual problem is. The human factor is important because a lot of this computer-generated German can mislead you. It makes arguments that the computer has thought up, but which aren't actually important for the people in question."

This can go to extremes: Friedrich-Johannes Graf von Pfeil, president of the social court in Potsdam, Brandenburg, has received one complaint that stretched to 800 pages.

"You can tell very quickly when one is AI-generated, just because they use specialist legal formulations that no ordinary citizen would use," he told DW. "There's often very little on the facts of the case, and a lot of legal interpretation that no non-specialist could provide. But you still have to respond to all of it."

The problem for judges is that they are obliged to wade through all this material, which often includes references to other legal rulings that either have little bearing on the case — or have been hallucinated by the AI tool.

Nor can the courts simply use their own AI tools to summarize these documents, von Pfeil said. "If we wanted to use AI to assess a legal document, we'd have security and data protection problems, because the AI isn't in-house," he said. "Also, we receive a lot of sensitive medical documents that would end up on a server that doesn't belong to the judiciary. And that's not allowed."

Could courts stem the flow with extra fees?

At a regular conference this month, Germany's state and federal justice ministers agreed to set up a working group to look into the problem, with some conservative ministers calling for a fee to file urgent complaints.

Christian Heinz, Christian Democrat justice minister in the state of Hesse, said that a fee of €15 ($16.40) should be considered. Another proposal was for people to pay court costs for lawsuits that are deemed to have little chance of success or which abuse the system.

The VdK, a social welfare association that offers legal advice to people dealing with German welfare authorities, is vehemently against those ideas. Holger Lange, head of the VdK's federal legal department, thinks it's vital that people — particularly the most vulnerable — have access to social courts without fearing the costs.

The solution, as far as Lange is concerned, is not to "build walls around the courts," but to streamline their digital access and make it easier to submit clear, concise complaints — in other words, online portals with easy-to-understand questions and word limits on legal documents. "They could steer the procedure a little," he told DW.

Howe is also skeptical of fees, an idea that, he said, has been discussed for decades. But social courts are supposed to have low thresholds to entry, he added: "This isn't a situation that suddenly justifies fees — yet. We want to keep access to justice open."

Judge von Pfeil thinks a fee would be "worth a try," though he acknowledges that a lot of people might apply for legal aid, which means the state would end up with more bureaucracy and costs anyway.

Is this even a real crisis?

Though there has been a recent increase in social court complaints, a broader look at the statistics shows that this is nothing that the social courts haven't seen before.

In the years leading up to the advent of wide availability of AI chatbots, the courts actually saw a big drop in the number of pending cases: from over 445,000 at the end of 2017 to 325,000 at the end of 2024. Analysts suggest that such long-term developments are tied to economic conditions and legal changes in unemployment benefits.

And Lange doesn't think that this new rise in complaints — AI-generated or not — is necessarily a bad sign. "The key thing is enabling people," he said. "We need to ask whether the recent rise isn't also in part the expression of a demand for legal protection that has been hidden so far, because people just haven't dared to claim their rights."

Lange acknowledged that AI-generated complaints can't always be trusted, because of errors and hallucinations. But he stressed that the use of AI doesn't make an appeal invalid.

"It could be a seriously ill person whose pension claim has just been refused," he said. "Or a care-dependent person who desperately needs support. We always need to look at who is behind the complaint."

entries.title: Azerbaijan's opposition leader Ali Karimli: A year behind bars
entries.summary: Azerbaijani opposition leader Ali Karimli has been in prison since November 2025. Authorities accuse him of attempting to seize power by force, but human rights groups say his prosecution is politically motivated.
entries.content:
Azerbaijan

Azerbaijan's opposition leader Ali Karimli: A year behind bars

November 28, 2026

Azerbaijani opposition leader Ali Karimli has been in prison since November 2025. Authorities accuse him of attempting to seize power by force, but human rights groups say his prosecution is politically motivated.

A year after his arrest, Azerbaijani opposition leader Ali Karimli remains in prison.

Karimli has denied charges of attempting to seize power by force, calling them politically motivated. He is the chairman of the Azerbaijani Popular Front Party (APFP), one of the country's main opposition parties.

Karimli is on trial alongside Mammad Ibrahim, his longtime political adviser and a senior party official. Ibrahim has previously served time in prison. In 2016, he was sentenced to three years on hooliganism charges that Human Rights Watch described as spurious. He was detained on November 29, 2025, alongside Karimli.

Amnesty: Government aims to 'crush all political opposition'

Azerbaijan's State Security Service has charged Karimli and Ibrahim under Article 278.1 of the Criminal Code, which covers actions aimed at forcibly seizing power or changing the country's constitutional order. A conviction could carry a prison sentence of 12 to 20 years, or life imprisonment.

In a statement issued on February 12, the State Security Service alleged that Karimli had conspired with the former head of Azerbaijan's Presidential Administration, Ramiz Mehdiyev, and his allies to seize state power. The agency also linked the alleged conspiracy to interference by foreign intelligence services in Azerbaijan's political affairs.

According to investigators, Karimli planned to exploit a mass rally in Baku in July 2020, originally held in support of the Azerbaijani army, to provoke unrest and seize the parliament and state television buildings. In a 15-page copy of a court motion obtained by DW from the APFP leadership, Karimli said he did not attend the rally and that his party was not involved in organizing it.

Nazim Musayev, a lawyer representing Mammad Ibrahim, told DW that both defendants considered the prosecution politically motivated. Shortly after the arrest, Amnesty International demanded that Azerbaijani authorities release Karimli "unless they can demonstrate reasonable evidence of an alleged criminal offence."

"Karimli's detention is the latest outrage in the ongoing consolidation of authoritarian practices in Azerbaijan," said Denis Krivosheev, Amnesty's deputy director for Eastern Europe and Central Asia, in a statement on December 1, 2025. "There appear to be no limits to the government's campaign to crush all political opposition and suppress all dissent in the country."

Trial behind closed doors

In the court motion obtained by DW, submitted at a preliminary hearing on November 3, Karimli made no secret of his desire for political change in Azerbaijan. However, he insisted he has always opposed using violence to achieve it.

"I accept only one way of coming to power — through democratic elections," Karimli wrote. The court rejected his call for charges to be dropped, but added the motion to his case file.

Karimli also disputed the prosecution's claims about the National Council of Democratic Forces, an opposition coalition formed in 2013. He said the group was established openly to support a joint opposition candidate in the presidential election rather than to organize a coup.

Karimli has also denied any cooperation with Mehdiyev, the ex-head of the presidential administration, saying the two have never met or communicated and that they represented opposing political positions for decades. Mehdiyev's lawyer told DW that his client also denies any connection to Karimli.

The trial against Karimli and Ibrahim is held behind closed doors, with foreign diplomats also being denied entry. Lawyer Nazim Musayev said the closed proceedings were justified on the grounds that the case involved state secrets.

In his motion, Karimli expressed little confidence in the fairness of the proceedings, argued that the case is intended to remove him from political life.

Rights groups raise alarm over Karimli's detention conditions

Karimli's son Turkel, who lives in the United States, told DW that he last spoke to his father in late April or early May. He said his mother had also been denied phone calls and face-to-face visits since June.

Turkel said his father's detention conditions had deteriorated sharply over the summer. Citing information received from lawyers, he said the authorities had temporarily stopped accepting food parcels from the family and restricted the amount of additional drinking water, which had been limited to 5 liters (1.3 gallons) a week. According to Amnesty International, Karimli reportedly fainted from severe dehydration during an August 6 court hearing.

Food deliveries were later permitted again, and lawyers were told earlier this month that the water allowance would be increased to 10 liters a week. Karimli's legal team said he has lost considerable weight during his time in prison.

Karimli has also complained of persistent noise disrupting his sleep, restrictions on family contact and physical exercise, worsening back pain and poor ventilation in his cell.

Rights groups have raised concerns about Karimli's detention conditions, with Amnesty International warning that the reported lack of access to clean drinking water and ventilation could amount to torture or other ill treatment.

Ibrahim's family reports health concerns

Ibrahim's family is concerned that he is not receiving adequate medical treatment in the detention facility. His son Turan Ibrahim, who lives abroad, told DW that his father suffers from kidney problems and insomnia.

According to Turan, doctors appointed by the authorities have examined his father several times. The family has also consulted outside doctors and is trying to arrange medication for him.

Turan said communication and family visits were sometimes difficult for his father. Ibrahim's wife delivers food and supplies to the detention facility once a week, and is allowed to see him through a glass partition twice a month.

Turan said his mother, who is unemployed and lives in rented accommodation, has also faced financial difficulties since her husband's arrest.

APFP opposition members also under scrutiny

Karimli has led the APFP since 2000. The party has continued operating during his detention.

Rahim Hajiyev, a founding member of the party who now lives in France, told DW that the APFP had long relied on collective decision-making and that Karimli's arrest had not brought its organizational activities to a halt.

However, he said party members, particularly those active on social media, continued to face short-term administrative detention. Hajiyev described Karimli's arrest as part of a broader campaign against political opposition.

EU calls for Karimli's immediate release

Karimli's detention has also drawn criticism from international organizations and European lawmakers.

On October 8, the European Parliament adopted a resolution calling for the immediate and unconditional release of Karimli and other political prisoners in Azerbaijan. Lawmakers also urged the authorities to ensure adequate medical care, access to lawyers and contact with family members. Earlier this month, Karimli was awarded the 2026 Magnitsky Human Rights Award.

Karimli's case was also raised at a joint press conference in Baku on November 18, attended by Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov and his German counterpart, Johann Wadephul. Asked about Karimli's arrest, Bayramov said that belonging to the opposition did not exempt anyone from legal responsibility.

Bayramov maintained that the case was being handled in accordance with Azerbaijani law and said the court would make the final decision.

entries.title: Ukraine's expertise comes in handy for international drone alliances
entries.summary: Ukrainian expertise merged with Europe's financial and industrial clout: Germany and other countries are expanding drone partnerships with Ukraine and reshaping Europe's defense industry in the process.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Ukraine's international drone alliances with Germany and others

November 28, 2026

Ukrainian expertise merged with Europe's financial and industrial clout: Germany and other countries are expanding drone partnerships with Ukraine and reshaping Europe's defense industry in the process.

Germany and Ukraine want to further boost their defense cooperation. Following a meeting in Berlin with his Ukrainian counterpart, Yevhenii Khmara, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius announced that drones for Ukraine will be manufactured in Germany in the future.

The project involves the Ukrainian reconnaissance drone known as the "Babka" ("Dragonfly"). Germany is investing around €34 million in the project, according to Pistorius. German company Wingcopter and Ukrainian manufacturer Shadow Flytech have established a joint venture specifically for this purpose.

A European 'Drone Alliance'

This is far from the first cooperation agreement of its kind that Kyiv has launched with its European partners. The initiatives include numerous joint ventures between Ukrainian companies and defense contractors across Europe.

In July 2026, the EU and Ukraine launched a joint "Drone Alliance." Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen reached an agreement to establish the initiative. The alliance focuses on joint development, industrial production, supply chains and counter-drone defense. One of its key goals is to combine Ukrainian technologies proven in combat with Europe's industrial production capabilities. The agreement on the Babka drones is also part of this alliance.

New bilateral agreements

As part of its Drone Deal strategy, Ukraine has sealed long-term bilateral agreements with several countries. These include the Netherlands, Norway, Finland and the Baltic states, as well as Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. Kyiv is also in negotiations with around a dozen other countries.

The cooperation covers four main areas: joint drone production; the exchange of intelligence and battlefield experience; cooperation in intelligence gathering, electronic warfare and cyber defense; and the training and advising of military personnel.

Although Germany has not yet formally joined the long-term Drone Deal framework, negotiations are afoot. German companies are already deeply involved in Ukraine's drone industry via several cooperation agreements.

This week, Ukraine and the United Kingdom also agreed on a new deal under which the UK will manufacture Ukrainian medium and long-range drones. In March, the two countries agreed to produce Ukraine's "Octopus" interceptor drone under license in the UK.

Rapid rise of the drone industry

Since the start of the war against Russia in the Donbas in 2014, Ukraine has developed a small but highly innovative drone industry. Up until 2022, however, the country only made a limited number of military drones.

With the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, development and production expanded dramatically. Before the full-scale war, only seven drone models had received state approval. By 2023, that number had risen to 67. By early 2024, around 200 companies were operating in Ukraine's drone sector.

"Perhaps some people underestimated the fact that Ukraine is not just an industrial country, but also a country of engineers, with a strong science and technology education system and a well-developed software industry," German security expert Nico Lange, director of the Berlin-based Institute for Risk Analysis and International Security (IRIS), told DW.

Ukraine has since massively expanded its domestic production capacity. According to Ukraine's Ministry of Defense, as of June 2026, 95% of the drones procured for its armed forces are now manufactured domestically.

The key question is whether Ukraine has sufficient funding, components and secure production facilities to meet demand over the long term.

Complicated supply chains, new projects

Drones are used at many levels of military operations. They come in various forms, including attack, interceptor and reconnaissance drones, and operate both in the air and at sea. They are significantly less expensive than many other weapons systems and, because of their small size and the sheer numbers in which they are deployed, can be difficult to defend against.

However, drones are mass-produced, and many of them, particularly small attack drones, are often destroyed after just a single mission or neutralized by electronic jamming.

In July 2026, Zelenskyy said Ukraine could manufacture around 10 million drones domestically each year. The goal, however, was to increase production to 20 million annually with support from European partners.

For a long time, supply chains remained a major challenge for Ukraine. As recently as early 2024, around 90% of all drone components — including motors, control chips and cameras — came from China.

"Traditionally, Chinese components have played an important role in the drone industry because of their lower cost," Nico Lange explains. "There are efforts to manufacture these components domestically, but that cannot happen overnight."

Through its defense cooperation agreements, Kyiv has managed to reduce the share of components imported directly from China to around 28% in the first eight months of 2026.

'Partnership between equals'

For Ukraine, access to Western supply chains for urgently needed components is a major benefit of the defense cooperation with Europe. Another advantage is that relocating production facilities abroad helps protect them from Russian attacks. Many of the agreements also provide for Ukraine to contribute the technology and battlefield experience, while its European partner supplies most of the funding and industrial capacity.

In the long run, however, Ukraine's most important reason for pursuing these partnerships is likely its ambition to establish itself as a lasting member of Europe's defense community and integrate its military into the European security architecture.

"What began as donations of weapons, ammunition and other equipment in the early stages of the war has evolved into a strategic partnership that offers significant benefits to both sides," says defense expert Lange. "It has rightly been described as a partnership between equals."

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: AI data centers in space: Millions of satellites and so many unknowns
entries.summary: SpaceX is seeking approval to launch a million satellites into orbit to build AI data centers in space. Experts are skeptical, citing many unanswered questions. At the top of the list: Who owns the sky?
entries.content:
November 28, 2026

SpaceX is seeking approval to launch a million satellites into orbit to build AI data centers in space. Experts are skeptical, citing many unanswered questions. At the top of the list: Who owns the sky?

Elon Musk's space company SpaceX has got the green light from the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) to build a network of 1 million satellites designed to host AI data centers in space. The project is called "Starmind."

Official approval comes with an ambitious timeline: SpaceX must have 10%, or 100,000, of the authorized satellites in orbit by 2035. By 2038, that figure must reach 50%. Within 15 years, a total of 1 million satellites are expected to orbit Earth, helping meet the rapidly growing demand for artificial intelligence computing power.

Why is space a potential location for AI data centers?

1. Ample sunshine and no clouds

"Putting data centers onto satellites and into space is somewhat attractive due to the higher availability of solar energy," Ulrich Speidel of the University of Auckland's School of Computer Science in New Zealand told the Science Media Center.

Depending on a satellite's orbit, it would be exposed to sunlight for more than half the day, Speidel said. And, of course, there are no clouds in space.

SpaceX makes a similar argument, saying its satellites would take advantage of space's plentiful energy and cooling possibilities, reducing the burden on Earth.

Electricity consumption by AI data centers is indeed rising worldwide. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), their consumption could more than double to 945 terawatt-hours per year by 2030. 

2. No water consumption for cooling

In addition to electricity, data centers on Earth consume large amounts of water to cool their servers. According to a recent study, global water consumption for this purpose ranges from 313 billion to 764 billion liters (82.7 billion to 201.8 billion gallons). Around a quarter of all data centers are also located in regions that regularly experience water shortages, the study's authors said.

Cooling in space, however, is difficult, Ulrich Speidel said. "The only way to remove heat from a satellite in a vacuum is to radiate it away, rather than dissipate it as we can do here on Earth using water or air cooling."

Richard Easther, a physicist at the University of Auckland, also sees cooling as a challenge, "but there are plausible solutions that are entirely consistent with basic physics."

However, Easther told the Science Media Center that the "Starmind" project is "at the very edge of technical feasibility." He also pointed out that Elon Musk's Starlink project would have sounded far-fetched 15 years ago.

What are the arguments against space as a location for AI data centers?

Easther said he sees the FCC timeline as unrealistic, joining others who doubt that SpaceX can meet its commitments to the agency.

"That would mean launching about eight satellites per hour from now until their deadline to complete the authorized constellation of Nov. 25, 2040," Laura Revell, a professor of atmospheric chemistry at the University of Canterbury in Christchurch, New Zealand, told the Science Media Center.

1. Rockets and satellites damaging the ozone layer

"I am extremely concerned about the levels of pollution that would accumulate in the atmosphere. We already know that emissions from rocket launches can cause depletion of the protective ozone layer," Revell said.

So far, this has not been a major problem because of the relatively small number of rocket launches. But this project could undo "decades of efforts to protect the ozone layer," she said.

The satellites themselves also pose an environmental risk, Revell said. Satellites are typically decommissioned after five years. When they reenter the atmosphere, they burn up, which "fundamentally turns the atmosphere into a crematorium for satellites," she said.

Overall, the long-term effects of vaporized metals on the atmosphere's climate and the ozone layer are entirely unknown.

2. Space debris on the rise

Space debris is already a problem. The Starmind project would increase the number of active satellites in orbit by more than 50-fold, Michael Brown, an astronomer at Monash University in Melbourne, Australia, told the Science Media Center.

"This greatly increases the risk of collisions with space junk, which could lead to the Kessler syndrome — a cascade of collisions that would make low Earth orbit unusable."

3. Light pollution in the night sky

Earth's increasingly crowded orbit is not the only factor that could make space research more difficult for astronomers in the future.

The Starmind satellites will come equipped with enormous solar panels. These will be larger and heavier than other satellites because of the cooling systems they need. This could have "devastating effects on numerous astronomical observations," physicist Richard Easther said. Even for people who are not astronomers, the view of the night sky could change dramatically.

The FCC made a decision with global implications on its own, dismissing environmental concerns as being "outside its purview," Laura Revell said.

"The question is, who has the authority to protect the upper atmosphere from rocket and satellite pollution for the common good?"

One thing is certain: Protecting the atmosphere should not be left to a company focused on maximizing profits.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: As Spain votes, what could change for Europe?
entries.summary: Spain votes on Sunday. A loss for Pedro Sanchez and a shift to the right in Madrid could affect how one of the EU's largest countries approaches migration, defense and the war in Gaza.
entries.content:
Spain

Spain's election could bring change for Europe

November 28, 2026

Spain votes on Sunday. A loss for Pedro Sanchez and a shift to the right in Madrid could affect how one of the EU's largest countries approaches migration, defense and the war in Gaza.

Walking through the halls of the European institutions in Brussels these days, it feels as if people are whispering about the end of an era. What happens when one of the most vocal leaders of Europe's center left is no longer at the table?

Pedro Sanchez is one of the few social democratic prime ministers left in the European Union, and Spain is the largest member state still led by one. That's why this election raises questions that go beyond who governs in Madrid.

After more than eight years in office Sanchez called a snap election at the beginning of October, three days after parliament rejected two emergency decrees aimed at tackling Spain's housing crisis. Anger over soaring housing costs has brought protesters onto the streets nationwide this year.

Sanchez's minority government was already under pressure over its handling of the summer migration crisis in Ceuta and accusations of corruption against his party and his wife, which both he and his wife have denied.

Polls on Monday predicted a tight race, putting the conservative People's Party (PP) at around 32% and the Socialists led by Sanchez at 31%.

With the right-wing populist Vox party in third place at around 17%, the polling projected an absolute majority for the PP and Vox combined. The two parties would still have to decide whether they want to govern together.

Important center-left voice may be 'silenced'

A change of government in Madrid would cost Europe's center left one of its most influential voices, Javier Carbonell, a policy analyst at the European Policy Centre in Brussels, told DW. "This voice might now be silenced."

Carbonell said three positions have set Sanchez apart: his willingness to challenge US President Donald Trump, his support for Palestinian statehood and his defense of immigration into Europe. Sanchez has been one of the few EU leaders who have continued to argue that migrant workers help fill labor shortages, support an aging Spanish and European population and sustain growth.

Earlier this year, his government opened a program to grant legal status to eligible migrants already living in Spain. It received more than 1 million applications. Spain's economy grew by 2.6% last year, nearly double the eurozone average, and the government expects GDP to grow by 2.6% this year and 2.2% in 2027.

Will Spain take a tougher line on migration?

The conservative PP has campaigned for tighter immigration controls while keeping routes open for workers in sectors facing shortages. Vox wants sharper cuts to immigration, more deportations and an end to regularization for new arrivals. It also wants Spanish citizens to get priority for subsidized housing and other social benefits.

This stance is nothing new at the European level. "With a PP-Vox government, Spain would join the general European trend towards an anti-immigration policy," said Carbonell, adding that he could see Madrid moving closer to countries pushing for tougher return policies. Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands are already in talks with Rwanda about setting up a hub for people whose asylum claims have been rejected.

Camino Mortera-Martinez, an associate fellow at the Centre for European Reform, agrees that a shift in Madrid would reinforce a trend already underway in Europe. "This anti-migration tendency doesn't come from European leaders, but from voters," she told DW.

PP, Vox back higher defense spending

Another domain where Spain could potentially change course and influence its European neighbors concerns its defense policies. Spain raised defense spending from 1.24% of GDP in 2024 to 2% in 2025, reaching NATO's previous benchmark.

Nevertheless, Sanchez has pushed back against the alliance's new annual target of 5% of GDP by 2035, which includes both military spending and broader security investments. He has argued that Spain could meet its NATO capability commitments by spending around 2.1% of GDP.

Both the PP and Vox favor higher defense investment but leave the exact figure open in their election programs. "They have a voting base that has no problem to increase defense spending, contrary to Sanchez," said Mortera-Martinez.

A shift on Israel and Palestinian statehood?

Mortera-Martinez also expects a change in Spain's approach to the Middle East, should Sanchez lose the election.

"The current government has been at the forefront of defending the last bastions of international and public law," she said.

Spain formally recognized a Palestinian state in May 2024. Sanchez has accused European leaders of applying double standards by rallying behind Ukraine against Russia's invasion, while failing to defend international law with the same resolve in the Middle East. In April, he pushed to suspend the EU's agreement with Israel, which makes respect for human rights an essential part of the relationship.

Carbonell, too, believes a new conservative government would be less vocal in its support for the Palestinians. "Sanchez was able to influence people on the subject matter, moving the consensus a bit more towards pro-Palestine," he said.

If Sanchez comes up short on Sunday, Europe's social democrats would lose their strongest foothold among the EU's largest countries. But, said Carbonell, a defeat in Spain could reignite a debate across the European center left about how to win back voters and stay politically relevant elsewhere.

entries.title: Germany news: Job market unlikely to recover before summer
entries.summary: The head of Germany's employment agency said employment would remain at its current level for a while. Meanwhile, electric vehicle sales are expected to pass 1 million next year. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Job market unlikely to recover before summer

Published November 28, 2026last updated November 28, 2026

The head of Germany's employment agency said employment would remain at its current level for a while. Meanwhile, electric vehicle sales are expected to pass 1 million next year. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Federal Employment Agency (BfA) chief says job market unlikely to recover before summer
  • German trade association predicts more than 1 million electric vehicle sales

Follow along for the top headlines and analysis from Germany on the Saturday, November 28 and Sunday, November 29:

Skip next section BSW leader defends limited cooperation with AfD

BSW leader defends limited cooperation with AfD

Sahra Wagenknecht, the leader of the left-wing populist Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW), formerly the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (also BSW), has spoken at her party's conference.

She defended the party's decision to work with the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), saying they needed to take advantage of the opportunity. 

"The AfD is a contradictory party," she said, adding: "But as long as there is a window of opportunity for concrete changes and improvements, we must make use of it."

The BSW's ambiguous relationship with the AfD has sparked debate within the party.

At the conference on Saturday, BSW co-founder Klaus Ernst threatened to leave the party if it didn't draw a clear line between itself and the far right.

Wagenknecht said it was not necessary for party members to "lecture each other about what unsavory characters can sometimes be found in the AfD and just how far this party is from us in terms of its platform."

Skip next section Some €16.5M paid out to victims of terror since Berlin attack

Some €16.5M paid out to victims of terror since Berlin attack

Germany has paid around €16.5 million ($18 million) to victims of terrorist and extremist attacks since the 2016 attack on the Berlin Christmas market, Federal Victim Commissioner Roland Weber has said.

"The number of people affected by these attacks is almost 3,000," Weber said.

Following the Berlin attacks alone, almost €4 million was paid out in hardship funds, according to the commissioner.

The Berlin attack was a turning point in such hardship funds, according to Weber, who said structures have been built up to respond to such situations since then.

The attack took place on December 19, 2016, when Tunisian man Anis Amri drove a truck into the middle of a busy Christmas market in the capital. Some 13 people were killed and another 109 were injured. Another 43 people, bereaved relatives, also received support.

Weber said that letters were quickly sent out to those impacted by a similar attack on a Christmas market in Magdeburg on December 20, 2024, letting them know that support was available.

Skip next section IN PICTURES: Winter has arrived in Germany

IN PICTURES: Winter has arrived in Germany

Skip next section Trade association predicts over 1M EV sales next year

Trade association predicts over 1M EV sales next year

The German Motor Trade Association (ZDK) predicts that more than 1 million electric vehicles will be sold in Germany in 2027.

The prediction was based on its estimate of 840,000 sales in 2026.

From January to October 2026, the Federal Motor Transport Authority recorded around 698,000 new all-electric cars.

The forecast also included a total of around 3.05 million passenger cars sold, up by 2.5%.

ZDK President Thomas Peckruhn said the electric car market would gain "further momentum" in 2027. "The range of models is growing, and government subsidies for electric cars can provide additional incentives to buy."

Skip next section Job market unlikely to recover until summer, employment agency warns

Job market unlikely to recover until summer, employment agency warns

Andrea Nahles, the head of the Federal Employment Agency (BfA), has warned that it could take months to see any noticeable recovery in the German job market.

She told the Funke media group that there would be little change between spring and early summer. Even if there's continued economic growth, its impact on the job market would be delayed.

"We've reached a tipping point," Nahles said. "For the first time, we're not seeing any growth in the number of employees subject to social insurance contributions, which currently stands at around 34 million."

She predicted that "demographics and the resulting worsening shortage of skilled workers will be the biggest problem facing the German labor market."

At the same time, there is no lack of unskilled workers. "There are currently 13 unemployed people for every open position for unskilled workers," she added.

At the same time, there are two jobs for every skilled worker.

The employment agency chief said it was necessary to attract more skilled immigrants.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from frosty Bonn.

You join us the day after the German Bundestag passed the government budget for 2027, even as EU budget talks in Brussels have been faltering.

Saturday is also the party convention for the left-wing populist BSW party.

For the latest on this and more, keep reading.

entries.title: Afghanistan: Several killed in blast near middle school
entries.summary: Officials have said improperly stored explosives at a mining site ignited, damaging nearby buildings including a school. An investigation is ongoing.
entries.content:
Afghanistan

Afghanistan: Several killed in blast near middle school

November 28, 2026

Officials have said improperly stored explosives at a mining site ignited, damaging nearby buildings including a school. An investigation is ongoing.

An explosion near a middle school on Saturday in Afghanistan's eastern Kunar province killed at least seven students and injured nearly 100 others, according to the Interior Ministry.

Early reports cited by the ministry's spokesperson indicate the blast was caused by negligent storage of explosives at a depot near the school belonging to a mining company in the Andir Sir area of the provincial capital, Asadabad.

No further details were provided on what caused the explosives to ignite.

Earlier, Kunar Provincial Police Headquarters spokesperson Farid Dehqan said the explosion occurred at around 10 a.m.

Unverified video footage posted on social media showed injured children being taken to the provincial hospital.

Samiulhaq Haqbayan, provincial director for information, told Germany's DPA news agency that the explosives were intended for use in mining operations and for clearing hazardous rocks from mountain slopes along the nearby Kunar-Nuristan highway.

Third blast near a school this week

The ministry said an investigation into the incident is ongoing and further details will be announced once it is completed.

Saturday's incident is the third explosion near educational facilities in Afghanistan in the past week.

Two separate blasts near religious schools in Kapisa and Farah provinces killed a total of five students, with local officials attributing both incidents to unexploded ordinances left behind from previous conflicts.

entries.title: India: Hindu lamp lighting at disputed Thiruparankundram pillar today
entries.summary: The Supreme Court has directed that the Tamil Hindu ceremonial Karthigai Deepam lamp be lit today at the disputed Deepathoon pillar. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
India

India: Tight security at disputed Deepathoon lamp-lighting ceremony

Published November 28, 2026last updated November 28, 2026

The Supreme Court has directed that the Tamil Hindu ceremonial Karthigai Deepam lamp be lit today at the disputed Deepathoon pillar. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

Here is our weekend coverage of India on Saturday, November 28:

  • A contentious stone pillar has stoked a legal, political and religious controversy in India’s Tamil Nadu

  • A Hindu ceremony will take place at the pillar today at the direction of the Supreme Court

  • An earlier order by the top court for the ritual lamp lighting to take place at the pillar was not followed

Skip next section READ — Indian workers fill Germany's labor gaps but face hurdles and risks

READ — Indian workers fill Germany's labor gaps but face hurdles and risks

The number of Indians working in Germany has grown rapidly in recent years. But many continue to face challenges in the labor market.

Some also fall victim to recruitment scams, leaving them vulnerable to exploitation.

Find out more in this report.

Skip next section Cricket: India 116-6 at stumps against New Zealand

Cricket: India 116-6 at stumps against New Zealand

New Zealand bowlers reduced India to 116 runs for 6 wickets at stumps on Saturday, on the second day of the second test cricket match at Christchurch’s Hagley Oval. 

The Black Caps saw a productive day in the series as they resumed at 246-5 from Friday, making a total of 356 runs in their first innings and then attacked India top batting order.

Kyle Jamieson bowled Yashasvi Jaiswal in the first over before dismissing Devdutt Padikkal at 21 runs and India's captain ‌Shubman Gill for 17 runs.

Fast bowler Jacob Duffy sent Rishabh Pant back to the pavilion with 23 runs and KL Rahul with 25.

Dhruv Jurel was 7 not out as the last ball of the day saw Washington Sundar out for 10 runs, caught by Tom Latham in slip off Nathan Smith.

Earlier, India pacer Akash Deep took 5-99 during New Zealand's innings.

It is now Deep's turn to bat as players come back to the ground on Sunday.

Skip next section Another Bisleri packaged water sample found 'unsafe' — reports

Another Bisleri packaged water sample found 'unsafe' — reports

India's food safety regulator found a sample of Bisleri packaged water "unsafe" due to the "presence of coliform bacteria," news agencies Reuters and PTI reported Saturday, citing unnamed sources.

Reuters cited a notice to Bisleri, reportedly dated August 12, where the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) asked the company to prohibit the sale of the specific batch over the finding.

Both the primary and referral laboratories had reported the presence of coliform bacteria in the sample, PTI said, citing sources.

Bisleri said in a statement to Reuters on Saturday that it had recalled the batch in question in August and that it had commissioned an independent testing of samples from the batch, which found the water meeting "the applicable standard for coliform bacteria and all other applicable food safety ​standards".

"The difference between the regulatory and independent findings warrants a thorough review," Bisleri told Reuters, adding that it would "continue to cooperate fully" with regulatory authorities to "establish the facts."

Saturday's reported finding is the second "unsafe" one surrounding the popular Indian packaged water brand, after the FSSAI said last week that a sample of Bisleri water did not meet prescribed limits of bromate, a potential carcinogen.

The body said that further tests of the sample detected polynuclear aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), a group of chemicals associated with pollution.

Bisleri questioned the findings and said that its water was safe for consumption.

Skip next section Supreme Court orders lamp lighting at Deepathoon, four days after festival

Supreme Court orders lamp lighting at Deepathoon, four days after festival

On Friday, the Supreme Court criticised the Tamil Nadu government and Madurai district officials for "wilful" defiance of the November 20 order and directed the lamp to be lit at Deepathoon on Saturday.

The Supreme Court suspended the Subramaniya Swamy temple's Board of Trustees and appointed a committee of two retired Madras High Court judges as receivers of the trust, who will oversee Saturday's ceremony.

The court also tweaked its earlier order and instead of a small team approved by the temple trust, has now permitted every devotee to light the lamp at Deepathoon on Saturday.

It has tasked the paramilitary CRPF with ensuring security at both the temple and the shrine ahead of the ceremony.

Skip next section Modi posts Tamil devotional chant amid Deepathoon row

Modi posts Tamil devotional chant amid Deepathoon row

Meanwhile, Prime Minister Narendra Modi wrote a post on X on last night, invoking Lord Murugan, one of the gods associated with Karthigai Deepam.

Without making any mention of the row, the Hindu nationalist leader wrote the traditional Tamil devotional chant "Victory to Lord Murugan, who wields the spear!" thrice, in English, Tamil and Hindi.

Skip next section Tamil Nadu: Lamp lighting at controversial Deepathoon site today amid security presence

Tamil Nadu: Lamp lighting at controversial Deepathoon site today amid security presence

Personnel of the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) were deployed at the Thiruparankundram hillock near Tamil Nadu state's Madurai, a day after the Supreme Court ordered a Hindu ceremonial lamp lighting to take place at a controversial stone pillar on Saturday.

At the heart of the row, is the Deepathoon (stone pillar) situated atop Thiruparankundram, and about 50 metres from the Hazrat Sultan Sikandar Badusha Auliya Dargah, a shrine associated with Sufism —  a mystical tradition within Islam. 

What is Tamil Nadu's stone pillar controversy?

The Arulmigu Subramaniya Swamy temple, also located on Thiruparankundram, traditionally conducts the annual Tamil Hindu Karthigai Deepam (festival of lights) ceremony at the Deepa Mandapam site near the Uchi Pillaiyar temple, situated on the lower part of the hill.

But Hindu groups had sought permission to light the ceremonial lamp at Deepathoon.

On November 20, India's top court permitted the lighting at Deepathoon as a one-time arrangement, allowing a restricted team to conduct the ceremony there.

However, the lamp was lit at the usual Deepa Mandapam when the festival came on November 24 as the temple trustees decided to stick to what they assert is established practice.

The Tamil Nadu government, helmed by Chief Minister C Joseph Vijay, also maintains that the customary spot for the ritual is near the Uchi Pillaiyar temple and had filed a review petition in the Supreme Court challenging its November 20 order.

Tuesday's lamp lighting led to protests by Hindu groups and also workers of theHindu Nationalist  Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which accused the Vijay government of refusing to comply with the Supreme Court's directive. 

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

This is Dharvi Vaid Dhulia from DW's studio in New Delhi, ushering you into India's newscape this weekend.

First, we dive into the developments coming out of the southern state of Tamil Nadu where a stone pillar is at the centre of political, legal and religious controversy.

Meanwhile there are rumblings in the power corridor of New Delhi as Prime Minister Narendra Modi's cabinet and his main rival, Congress party, have held meetings respectively, to talk tactics ahead of a sudden, special sitting of the parliament called at the request of the ruling government.

And India's Men in Blue are facing New Zealand's Black Caps for a second day of a high-stakes test cricket match at Hagley Oval in Christchurch.

Stay tuned as we bring you more.

entries.title: Indian workers fill Germany's labor gaps but face hurdles and risks
entries.summary: The number of Indians working in Germany has grown rapidly in recent years. But many continue to face challenges in the labor market. Some also fall victim to recruitment scams, leaving them vulnerable to exploitation.
entries.content:
November 28, 2026

The number of Indians working in Germany has grown rapidly in recent years. But many continue to face challenges in the labor market. Some also fall victim to recruitment scams, leaving them vulnerable to exploitation.

Pratyay Saikia was studying food technology in 2022 when he saw an advertisement from Magic Billion, a recruitment agency that places skilled and semi-skilled Indian professionals in verified jobs abroad.  

The 25-year-old from the northern Indian state of Haryana reached out to explore employment opportunities.

Four years later, he is working as a butcher at Metzgerei Lederer in southern Germany, having completed a three-year apprenticeship at the butcher shop.

"I came to Baden-Württemberg with 180 other Indians who came here to do an Ausbildung [apprenticeship] program. Me and seven others did our Ausbildung at Lederer [butcher shop], while others went into the construction sector. I now have a full-time job here," Saikia told DW.

He is not alone as the number of Indian workers subject to social security contributions in Germany has grown sevenfold over the past decade, to over 140,000 professionals.

Many of them work in the IT and health care sectors.

Pressing need for workers, but hesitant to hire

Germany, facing a shrinking and rapidly aging population, doesn't just need software specialists and nurses. It is also seeking skilled professionals such as electricians, mechatronics technicians, solar panel installers and truck drivers.

A 2024 study by Bertelsmann Foundation concluded that Germany needs 288,000 foreign skilled workers per year until 2040 to fill the shortage left by retiring workers. Another report from the consulting firm FMC Group noted that over 369,000 skilled job positions went unfilled in 2025.

Despite the pressing need for skilled workers, many firms, particularly Germany's renowned Mittelstand (small and medium-sized enterprises), are reluctant to recruit from places like India, say observers.   

"Hiring an electrician from India is a relatively new concept for German companies, so they are hesitant," said Daniel Raja, managing director of NM NextMittelstand GmbH, a Düsseldorf-based recruitment firm focused on connecting German firms with skilled workers from India.

The Mittelstand companies are often overlooked by young talent abroad, while many of these firms are not actively recruiting international skilled workers, Raja said.

This disconnect, coupled with the often high German language requirements, means that many skilled positions remain unfilled, he explained.

Language a key hurdle

Saikia, the butcher, had studied German to the B1 level, considered intermediate proficiency. He soon realized it was not enough for everyday communication at work.

"Initially, I found the theory classes of my Ausbildung quite difficult. But my co-workers helped me. After one year, my German improved, and I realized integration happened automatically as my language level improved," he said.

David Kipp, researcher in the Global Issues Research Group at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs (SWP), said he's "skeptical" about lowering language requirements.

"Language skills are an important selection criterion so people actually know where they are going. Sending people with very little language knowledge makes exploitation easier, because they have less direct contact with German institutions," he told DW.

Language, however, isn't the only hurdle.

Raja said workers' councils also often resist hiring from abroad.

"Company decisions in the Mittelstand involve the team and the shop floor," he pointed out. "In some cases, the workers' council resists hiring from India because they mistakenly believe 'cheap Indian labor' will take their jobs or undercut their wages."

Raja said he often uses unconventional outreach methods, including hosting TikTok Live sessions, to engage directly with industrial employers and workers and dispel concerns and misconceptions.

Exploiting the EU mobility loophole?

German companies have traditionally relied on workers from Central and Eastern European (CEE) nations such as Poland, Romania and Slovenia to fill labor market gaps.

But studies show CEE workers are increasingly reluctant to relocate to Germany, as faster economic growth and stronger career prospects improve opportunities in their home countries.

The situation has prompted recruitment agencies in these countries to look beyond the European Union for workers.

These third-country nationals (TCNs) obtain residence permits in CEE states and are then posted to German job sites under the Vander Elst visa. The mechanism allows non-EU citizens legally employed in one EU member state to be temporarily sent to work in another.

"European Labour Authority's (ELA) 2025 study on the posting of third-country nationals found that the number of posted TCNs is increasing. The main sectors concerned are construction and transport," said Pia Fallstrom, ELA spokesperson.

The exact number of TCNs posted across the EU is difficult to gauge, as data exchange between sending and receiving countries by nationality and sector is limited.

"Finding out how blue-collar workers get here really requires fieldwork," said Kipp, noting that Indian recruiters are aware of this mobility loophole and take advantage of these opportunities.

While there are regulations to protect workers posted to Germany from another EU state, ELA said the practice has often led to wage-dumping.

"ELA's work has identified issues such as difficulties accessing information on applicable rules, complex subcontracting arrangements, letterbox companies, bogus self-employment and other cases of non-compliance," noted Fallstrom.

"Posted third-country nationals can be particularly vulnerable because they may also depend on their employer for their work and residence permits."

Raja said he had seen cases of workers falling victim to recruitment scams and being exploited as a result.

"I know of a family that took out a loan so that their child could enroll in an institute which promised a job in Germany," said Raja. "When the candidate realized it's a scam, they ended up in Bahrain doing a tough manual labor job just to pay off the loan."

What to do to prevent exploitative hiring practices?

Saikia, the butcher, stressed the importance of workers verifying that a recruitment agency is legitimate.

In his case, he said the agency's detailed website and its CEO's willingness to speak with him during the early stages of the recruitment process gave him confidence that it was not a scam.

Kipp, the SWP expert, argued that preventing exploitative hiring practices requires streamlining migration procedures, expanding pre-departure cultural training and becoming more effective at identifying trusted entities and combating social media scams.

"India is the most important country for experimenting with how work migration functions. If we don't pay attention, we'll just send people into the low-wage sector and into disappointment," he said.

entries.title: Taiwan election: DPP gains ground but loses Taipei race
entries.summary: Taiwan's ruling DPP has made gains in local elections, winning nine of 22 local governments. But it failed to retake Taipei, where incumbent KMT Mayor Chiang Wan-an defeated challenger Puma Shen.
entries.content:
Taiwan

Taiwan's ruling DPP makes local election gains, fails to retake Taipei

November 28, 2026

Taiwan's ruling DPP has made gains in local elections, winning nine of 22 local governments. But it failed to retake Taipei, where incumbent KMT Mayor Chiang Wan-an defeated challenger Puma Shen.

Taiwan's ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) made gains in local elections on Saturday, winning nine of the island's 22 local governments, up from five in 2022.

The opposition Kuomintang (KMT) secured 12 local governments, two fewer than in the previous elections, while the Taiwan People's Party (TPP) won one city, according to local media reports.

The elections, in which voters chose mayors and county chiefs for four-year terms, are being seen as an indication of the political mood ahead of the island's 2028 presidential elections.

President Lai Ching-te campaigned for DPP candidates, while the KMT, which traditionally performs better in local polls and favours closer ties with China, sought to retain its local strongholds.

Closely watched Taipei mayor race goes to KMT

In the most closely watched contest, incumbent Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an of the KMT defeated DPP challenger Puma Shen, ending the ruling party's hopes of regaining control of the capital for the first time since 1998.

Shen conceded defeat in front of thousands of supporters, saying the voters' decision must be respected.

"Whoever wins, it is a victory for Taiwan's democracy," he told supporters.

Chiang thanked voters for backing his administration, saying they had recognised the city's work over the past four years.

China is paying close attention to the local polls, despite not currently featuring as a key campaign issue. Taiwan's government had warned its people to be vigilant against fake news on social media, citing a Chinese disinformation campaign. 

Taiwan's 22 cities and counties are currently focused on issues such as transport, childcare and the environment. While these issues do not directly impact the China policy, Beijing has repeatedly weighed in.

China has denounced DPP candidate Puma Shen, who was sanctioned by Beijing and is wanted by Chinese police over alleged separatist activities.

He entered the mayoral race as an underdog but had managed to ride a political wave that drew huge crowds to his campaign rallies.

Nevertheless, the DPP announced Saturday evening that Shen had lost his bid for mayor, which was seen as a longshot as Taipei has not elected a DPP mayor in nearly 30 years.

Earlier this month, Shen said Chinese police had never contacted him and that whoever wins, Taipei's election would be a victory for democracy in the face of pressure from Beijing.

Taipei turning to a progressive candidate in what has traditionally been a KMT stronghold would be seen as "quite shameful" in Beijing, Austin Wang, political science professor at the University of Nevada, told AFP news agency.

China claims Taiwan as part of its territory under its "One China" principle and has recently increased pressure on Taiwan to accept its sovereignty claims, threatening force to seize the island. 

Mayor Chiang campaigned against Shen, also pulling in thousands of supporters to his rallies. Chiang is seen as a potential future presidential candidate.

What impact could the vote have on presidential elections?

Analysts have cautioned that the local elections are not a reliable barometer of how people might vote for the presidential elections in 2028. Still, Saturday's results could influence the selection process for the KMT presidential candidate.

The DPP is likely to rally behind President Lai for a reelection.

The most likely KMT candidates are Taichung's outgoing Mayor Lu Shiow-yen and parliamentary speaker Han Kuo-yu.

KMT Chairwoman Cheng Li-wun, who's pro-Beijing stance has even alienated her from many in the party, is also viewed as a potential challenger for the party's nomination. However, she could face pressure to step down if KMT performs poorly in the local elections.
